newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Meyer says U.S. economy really strong.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Meyer says U.S. economy really strong.

text.p: Federal Reserve Governor Laurence Meyer said the economy was really strong and its performance was not a "fluke."
"The economy is really strong," Meyer told the Washington Post in an interview. "This is not a fluke."
The Post article said Meyer would not comment directly on what the Fed might do at its next monetary policy meeting on May 20.

The U.S. central bank last week increased interest rates for the first time in more than two years, bumping up its target for the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.5 percent from 5.25 percent.

The Post, paraphrasing Meyer, said it was the combination of the already low jobless rate and the unexpectedly strong growth that threatened to drive it even lower that caused him to decide a rate increase was necessary last week.
The risk was raised that the nation's labor markets would become so tight that inflationary pressures were sure to increase, though that hadn't happened yet.
"There is no way of rationalizing this except by what the (Fed) chairman (Alan Greenspan) has emphasized: It's a forward-looking policy," Meyer said.
On Tuesday, a trio of economic reports showed signs of a strengthening economy.
The National Association of Purchasing Management found that manufacturing activity expanded at its highest rate in more than two years.
Separately, the Commerce Department said spending on new construction increased in February at the briskest rate in nearly a year.
A third report from the Conference Board showed its broad-based index of leading indicators up 0.5 percent in February, indicating continuing growth ahead.
The Post said that as a result of such numbers, many analysts - as well as Fed officials - had been revising upward their growth forecasts for the first half of this year.
Meyer said he was not opposed to strong growth or substantial wage gains, but rather to levels of either that would lead to higher inflation.

He would be "looking for evidence" ahead of the May 20 meeting on the speed of growth, utilization rates for resources such as labor, whether wage gains are accelerating and whether inflation itself is rising.
